analysis.one_liner: Lets a single company own TV stations reaching up to 40% of the national audience, up from 35%.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House committee without ever getting a vote, so the 35% national TV ownership limit stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the FCC to let one company own TV stations that reach 40% of the national TV audience, instead of the current 35% limit, with possible increases to 45% or 50% tied to programs that raise minority ownership of stations. It would also have required the FCC to study how higher ownership limits affect small and minority-owned station businesses, and to give first pick of newly available broadcast spectrum to applicants promising non-English programming or service to underserved communities. The bill never got past a House committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Large television station owners and broadcast networks, which could buy or combine more stations and reach a bigger share of the national audience under the higher cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large TV station owners and networks

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the FCC to raise the national audience reach limit for TV station ownership from 35% to 40%, letting a single owner's stations reach a larger share of viewers nationwide.

The limit could climb further, by 5% and then possibly another 5%, when the FCC finds that a private or government program has increased ownership of TV stations by members of minority groups, an approach the bill describes as reducing restrictions on ownership while improving diversity of ownership.

The bill requires the FCC to give priority, in assigning newly returned broadcast spectrum, to applicants that commit to broadcasting in a language other than English or representing traditionally underserved communities.
The bill directs the FCC to study and report to Congress on how raising the ownership limit affects the ability of small businesses and minority group members to enter television broadcasting.

analysis.who_pays: Viewers, who would have fewer independent owners shaping local and national TV news, and smaller or prospective station owners, who would face bigger consolidated competitors.

drawbacks.text: Raising the national cap to 40%, and potentially to 50%, would have allowed one company to reach nearly half the national TV audience, reducing the number of independent voices deciding what viewers see.

The diversity mechanism is indirect: bigger owners gain more reach only if outside programs happen to raise minority ownership, so the bill offers no guarantee that consolidation would actually expand minority ownership, only a study of the effect after owners reach the new limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's concrete, immediate benefit goes to the largest station owners, while its diversity benefits are contingent and unproven — an FCC study would only happen after owners reach the higher limit. An honest supporter could argue the trade links consolidation to minority ownership gains, but the structure rewards big owners first and leaves the public-interest gains speculative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Telecommunications Subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel introduced the bill on November 17, 1999, joined by Reps. Bobby Rush and Sheila Jackson-Lee.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On December 3, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, and no further action was recorded before the Congress ended in January 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained the loosened cap; the existing 35% ownership limit and the rules around it stayed in place, which left small station owners and the diversity of station ownership unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; big owners gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Eliot Engel
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to raise the national TV ownership cap and add the minority-ownership and spectrum-priority provisions.

for.name: Reps. Bobby Rush and Sheila Jackson-Lee

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Telecommunications Subcommittee and never took it up for a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but no committee or floor votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Large broadcast station owners and TV networks
industries.note: The bill's immediate effect would raise the share of the national TV audience a single owner can reach from 35% to 40%, and up to 50% if its diversity conditions trigger, letting the biggest owners grow. Fewer independent owners means less local control of TV news, which costs viewers even as it rewards the industry.

industries.industry: Minority-owned and small broadcast businesses, and non-English and community broadcasters
industries.note: The bill requires an FCC study of how the higher cap affects small and minority entry into broadcasting and gives returned spectrum priority to non-English and underserved-community applicants. But loosening ownership caps generally makes entry harder for small players, so the bill both offers and threatens them.
